questions.question: What does the Java compiler javac produce from a .java source file?
options: A .class file holding bytecode
An .exe file holding machine code for this computer
A running program, started as soon as compiling finishes
A tidied .java file with comments and spacing removed
questions.explanation: javac translates your source into bytecode and writes it to a .class file. It stops there: bytecode is not machine code for any particular processor, and nothing runs until you start a JVM.

questions.question: Which piece of software takes a compiled .class file and actually runs it?
options: javac, the Java compiler
The JVM, the Java Virtual Machine
javadoc, the documentation generator
The operating system, which runs bytecode directly
questions.explanation: The JVM loads the .class file and executes its bytecode. The compiler's job ended when the .class file was written, and an operating system cannot execute bytecode on its own: it needs a JVM built for that platform.

questions.question: What is the JDK?
options: The Java Development Kit: the toolkit for writing and compiling Java
The program that executes bytecode, with a separate build per platform
An editor, debugger and file browser bundled into a single application
The collection of .class files produced when a program is compiled
questions.explanation: The JDK is what you install to develop Java: it carries the compiler javac, tools such as javadoc, and a runtime to execute what you build. The program that executes bytecode is the JVM, which is one part of the kit rather than the whole of it.

questions.question: Java is described as write once, run anywhere. What does that mean in practice?
options: The same source file has to be recompiled on every platform it runs on
A Java program can be written in any programming language you like
The same bytecode file runs on any platform that has a JVM
A Java program runs without any software being installed first
questions.explanation: You compile once, to bytecode, and every platform's own JVM runs that identical file. Recompiling per platform is exactly what write once, run anywhere avoids, and the target machine still needs a JVM installed.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: Hello, World!
"Hello, World!", including the double quotes
HelloPrinter
Nothing, because nothing in the file calls main
questions.explanation: println writes the text between the quotes and then moves to a new line; the quotes themselves only mark where the text starts and ends, so they are not printed. main does not need calling by your code: the JVM starts the program by calling it for you.

questions.question: Roughly how many reserved keywords does the Java language have?
options: About 15
About 120
Over 500
questions.explanation: Java reserves 50 keywords, a small enough set to fit on one page, and two of them (const and goto) are reserved without being used at all. Familiar words such as String and main are not keywords: they are ordinary names from the standard library and from your own code.

questions.question: Why does this program fail to compile?
options: The statement is missing the semicolon that ends it
print should be used instead of println for text
The message must be in single quotes rather than double quotes
system is not System, and Java treats those as different names
questions.explanation: Java is case-sensitive, so the lowercase system does not name the System class; the compiler instead goes looking for a package called system and reports that no such package exists. The semicolon is present and the quotes are correct: only the capital S is missing.

questions.question: What is an IDE?
options: A cloud service that runs finished programs on behalf of their users
A single application bundling the tools for writing and running code
The part of the JDK that turns your source code into bytecode
A file format that stores a program's source and its output together
questions.explanation: An Integrated Development Environment gathers an editor, a compiler, a way to run the program and a debugger into one place: Eclipse, NetBeans, IntelliJ and VS Code are common examples. It automates the compile-and-run steps you could otherwise type by hand, but the compiler itself still comes from the JDK.

questions.question: One of these lines stops the program compiling. Which one, and why?
options: Line 1, because the first statement of a program cannot print
Line 2, because it is missing the semicolon that ends a statement
Line 3, because the last statement of a block needs no semicolon
None of them: the end of a line also ends a statement in Java
questions.explanation: Every Java statement ends in a semicolon, and line 2 has none, so the compiler never sees where that statement stops. A line break means nothing to the compiler: only the semicolon marks the boundary between one statement and the next.

questions.question: Working in a console, which command asks the compiler to turn HelloPrinter.java into HelloPrinter.class?
options: javac HelloPrinter.java
javadoc HelloPrinter.java
java HelloPrinter
compile HelloPrinter.java
questions.explanation: javac is the compiler, and you hand it the source file complete with its .java ending. The separate command java HelloPrinter is the next step: it starts a JVM and gives it the bytecode to run.

questions.question: What does an interpreter do?
options: It translates the whole program into machine code before any of it runs
It rewrites a program from one programming language into another
It executes the instructions directly, with no separate compiled program
It checks a program for spelling and layout mistakes before compiling
questions.explanation: An interpreter reads instructions and carries them out as it goes, so no compiled program is produced along the way. Translating everything into machine code up front is the compiler's job, and mixing those two definitions up is the usual trap here.

questions.question: Java is often described as both compiled and interpreted. Why?
options: The source is interpreted line by line, then the results are saved as a .class file
Some statements are compiled and the rest interpreted, depending on the keyword used
The compiler produces machine code, which the JVM then reads back as text
The source is compiled to bytecode ahead of time, and the JVM then runs it
questions.explanation: Java stops halfway: javac compiles ahead of time, but only as far as bytecode, and the JVM takes over from there to execute it. Nothing about your source depends on which keywords you used, and the compiler never produces machine code for a particular processor.

questions.question: What happens when this program is compiled?
options: It compiles and prints Report ready, since ou is close enough to out
Compile error: the compiler cannot find any symbol named ou in System
It compiles, but nothing at all appears when the program is run
Compile error: println must always be called on System, never on out
questions.explanation: The compiler matches names exactly, so ou simply does not exist and it reports cannot find symbol. A compiler never guesses at what you meant or corrects a misspelling for you, which is why one dropped letter stops the build.

questions.question: You compiled HelloPrinter.java on a Windows machine. A friend using macOS wants to run your program. What should you send, and what do they need?
options: Send HelloPrinter.java; they must recompile it with a macOS compiler first
Send both files, because macOS can only start a Java program from its source
Send HelloPrinter.class; they need a JVM built for macOS
Send HelloPrinter.class; it will not run, as it holds Windows machine code
questions.explanation: Bytecode belongs to no platform, so the .class file you built on Windows is exactly the file a Mac needs, and no recompiling is involved. The JVM is the platform-specific part, which is precisely what lets your program avoid being platform-specific.

questions.question: This code is saved in a file named Greeting.java. What happens when that file is compiled?
options: It compiles, and the bytecode is written to Greeting.class
Compile error: a public class must sit in a file of the same name
It compiles, and the source file is renamed HelloPrinter.java for you
It compiles, but the JVM cannot find main when the program is started
questions.explanation: A public class named HelloPrinter has to live in HelloPrinter.java, so the compiler rejects the file outright rather than compiling it under either name. Renaming the file, or renaming the class, fixes it; the compiler will not choose for you.

questions.question: What happens when this program is compiled?
options: It compiles and prints Started, since main hands back no value anyway
Compile error: a method declaration with no return type is not valid
It compiles, but nothing is printed when the program is started
Compile error: a method named main may not take any parameters
questions.explanation: Every Java method states a return type, and main's is void, so leaving that one word out of public static void main(String[] args) makes the declaration invalid and the compiler asks for a return type. It is tempting to think void can be dropped because main returns nothing, but void is precisely how you say that.

questions.question: What happens when this program is compiled?
options: It prints Ada, because Java ignores capitalisation inside a name
Compile error: cannot find symbol, as name and Name are different names
It prints nothing, because name has not been given a value yet
Compile error: a variable name is not allowed to start with a capital letter
questions.explanation: Case carries meaning everywhere in Java, so Name and name identify two entirely different variables and only one of them was ever declared. A capital first letter is unconventional for a variable but perfectly legal: the error is the mismatch, not the capital.

questions.question: A platform is a hardware device plus the operating system running on it. Why can one .class file run on Windows, macOS and Linux without being changed?
options: The .class file carries a separate copy of the machine code for each platform
Every modern operating system can execute bytecode without any extra software
The .class file is plain text, which each platform compiles as the program runs
Bytecode belongs to no platform, and each platform has its own JVM to run it
questions.explanation: Machine code is married to one platform, but bytecode is married to none, so the single .class file suits them all. The variation is pushed into the JVM instead: there is a different JVM per platform, each running that same unchanged bytecode.

questions.question: What does the compiler report for this file?
options: reached end of file while parsing: a closing brace is missing
cannot find symbol, because total is never declared anywhere
missing return statement, because main must return a value
Nothing at all: the compiler supplies any brace you leave out
questions.explanation: Two braces are opened, for the class and for main, and only one is closed, so the compiler runs out of file while still waiting for the class to end. Unmatched braces are the classic case where the error is reported at the last line even though the mistake is further up.

questions.question: Three of these words are Java keywords. Which one is not?
options: class
static
main
void
questions.explanation: main is just a name, chosen because the JVM looks for a method called that when it starts a program; you are free to name other methods main too. class, static and void are reserved keywords, so they can never be used as a name of your own.

questions.question: Under what name, and at which company, was Java originally developed?
options: Oak, at Sun Microsystems
Oak, at Oracle Corporation
Coffee, at Sun Microsystems
J++, at Microsoft
questions.explanation: James Gosling designed the language at Sun Microsystems in 1991 and called it Oak, after the tree outside his window, before it was renamed Java. Oracle is easy to name here because it stewards Java today, but it only acquired Sun in 2010, long after the language existed.

questions.question: What does the JVM do with the bytecode in a .class file?
options: It reads your .java source line by line and carries out each line as it goes
It turns the bytecode back into Java source, which it then compiles and runs
It executes the bytecode, interpreting it and compiling the hot parts
It hands the bytecode to the operating system, which then executes it directly
questions.explanation: The JVM is the thing that runs your program: it interprets bytecode instruction by instruction and also compiles the parts that run often into machine code, so a long-running program speeds up. It never sees your source, which javac already consumed, and an operating system cannot execute bytecode itself.

questions.question: The compiler rejects this code, saying a semicolon was expected. What has it done with the two lines?
options: It ignored the first line, because a statement with no semicolon is skipped
It joined them into one run-on statement, since only a semicolon ends one
It read two statements and rejected the second one as unreachable code
It read two statements but needs a blank line separating them
questions.explanation: The compiler uses the semicolon, never the line break, to find where a statement ends, so it reads straight past the end of the first line and meets a second call where it expected a semicolon. Nothing is ever quietly skipped: a statement the compiler cannot make sense of stops the build.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes how the JDK, the JRE and the JVM relate to each other?
options: The JVM contains the JDK, so installing a JVM also installs the compiler
The JRE contains the JDK, which supplies the compiler and the runtime
The JDK and the JRE are two names for exactly the same download
The JDK holds the development tools plus a runtime containing the JVM
questions.explanation: The JDK is the outermost box: it holds the tools you develop with and a runtime environment whose centre is the JVM. A runtime on its own can only run programs, so a machine carrying just the JRE can execute a .class file but cannot compile one.

questions.question: You run javac Broken.java on this file and the compiler reports an error. Which files are in the folder afterwards?
options: Broken.java only, as no class file is written when compiling fails
Broken.java and Broken.class, with the faulty line left out of the bytecode
Broken.java and Broken.class, because javac always writes its output file
Broken.class only, because javac replaces the source with its output
questions.explanation: A failed compile produces no bytecode, so there is nothing for the JVM to run and java Broken would report that the class cannot be found. The source file is never consumed or altered by compiling: add the missing semicolon and run javac again.

questions.question: Java reserves the words goto and const but gives them no meaning in the language. What happens if you try to name a variable goto?
options: It works, because a word with no meaning in Java is free to use as a name
It works, but the compiler prints a warning about the chosen name
It works only when the variable is declared inside a method
Compile error, because a reserved word can never be used as a name
questions.explanation: Reserved means reserved whether or not the word does anything: goto and const are held back so that no program can ever claim them, and the compiler rejects both as names. Where you declare the variable makes no difference, and no compiler will accept the name with a warning.
